topic: Bayer filter / demosaicing: 2/3 of every photo's color is interpolated
lines: Two thirds of every photo you've ever taken... is made up.
Two thirds of every photo you've ever taken... is made up.
It only measures how much light hits each pixel.
So in nineteen seventy-six, a Kodak engineer named Bryce Bayer patented a trick.
So in 1976, a Kodak engineer named Bryce Bayer patented a trick.
Put a tiny color filter over every single pixel.
Red, green, or blue. Only one.
But look closer. Half of them are green.
A twenty-four megapixel camera has twelve million green pixels,
A 24 megapixel camera has 12 million green pixels,
but only six million red, and six million blue.
but only 6 million red, and 6 million blue.
Why? Because your eyes are tuned to green.
It carries about seventy percent of the brightness you see.
It carries about 70% of the brightness you see.
So each pixel measures one color,
and guesses the other two from its neighbors.
And when it guesses wrong, you get these rainbow artifacts.
In every pixel, of every photo you've ever taken.

youtube.title: 2/3 of Every Photo You've Ever Taken Is Made Up
youtube.description:
Your camera sensor can't see color. Every pixel sits under ONE red, green or blue filter (the Bayer filter, patented by Bryce Bayer at Kodak in 1976), and the other two colors are guessed from its neighbors. That's demosaicing.
Half the filters are green because green carries ~72% of the brightness you perceive (ITU-R BT.709).
The rainbow demo is a real simulation: a zone plate run through a Bayer mosaic + bilinear demosaicing.
(Foveon sensors skip this; Fujifilm X-Trans uses a different pattern.)
